transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Meeting id: starlake-20261202-0043
Attendees: Jess Carter (Redwood AE), Marco Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Starlake Head of ML), Tomás Alvarez (Platform Eng), Rene Cho (InfoSec)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Starlake's model needs: open-model comparisons, long-context requirements (some flows up to 200k tokens), multilingual support (EN, ES, FR, PT), tool-calling for data pulls and SQL generation, and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC). Security and auditability are top-tier requirements.

---
[00:00] Jess (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros, then Marco will dig into the technical bits.
[00:18] Priya (Starlake): Hi, Priya here, I run the ML org. We own the models; Tomás and Rene are on the call for infra and security questions.
[00:27] Tomás (Starlake): Tomás, platform eng. We're evaluating cost/latency tradeoffs and integration complexity.
[00:35] Rene (Starlake): Rene, InfoSec. I'll be focused on data residency, KMS, audit logs, and SOC 2.
[00:42] Marco (Redwood SE): Great. We'll cover model choices, quantization options, context length, multilingual behavior, and tool-calling. Also can run a pilot to compare hosted vs dedicated.
[01:05] Priya: Thanks. A few clarifying things up front — our main production flows are a multilingual agent that converses with users and calls internal services (search, billing, SQL), and a long-document summarization pipeline — docs can be 50k to 200k tokens. We also do fine-grained reranking for search.
[01:30] Jess: Perfect, that give us a good lens. Tomás, what's your current infra? Cloud + self-managed data platform?
[01:38] Tomás: We're mainly on GCP with a hybrid of on-prem proprietary storage for PII. We use Cloud KMS and a corporate SSO (SAML). Network egress is a compliance concern.
[01:50] Rene: Also need audit trails per-request, retention policy of 7 years for some logs, and the ability to restrict model outputs from being logged in plaintext for certain classes.
[02:05] Marco: Understood. Redwood Private in a VPC or on-prem option can keep requests in your network; we also support customer KMS/HSM integrations for key material and can redact or not persist full prompts per route. We have per-token audit logs and can stream them to your SIEM.
[02:30] Priya: How does Redwood handle really long contexts? Traditional chunking hits latency and cost hard.
[02:40] Marco: Two levers: first, our serving runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching to avoid re-encoding repeated context; second, we recommend model variants tuned for long-context (e.g. specialized open models with chunked attention or sparse attention mechanisms). For extreme lengths — 100k+ tokens — we typically recommend a hybrid approach: retrieval + condensed context + embeddings for the rest.
[03:08] Priya: Are there open models that handle 200k tokens well out of the box?
[03:15] Marco: Not many robustly. Some research variants can, but they have tradeoffs on quality. We often route long-context requests to a model variant with extended positional encoding and use summarization to keep token budgets reasonable. Also, Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization+batching profiles to control cost.
[03:40] Jess: On the commercial side, we can provision Dedicated pools with predictable throughput and reserved commits, or you can start on Hosted to validate quality. Private deployment is possible if you need full control.
[03:57] Tomás: Latency SLOs matter — sub-400ms for short chat replies, but longer is acceptable for summarization. How predictable is latency on hosted?
[04:10] Marco: Hosted gives fast onboarding and low cold-starts, but Dedicated gives tighter latency tails with reserved GPU capacity. We also have routing policies — e.g., route low-priority batch jobs to cheaper quantized variants.
[04:28] Rene: About compliance: SOC 2? ISO? SSO?
[04:32] Jess: We're SOC 2 Type II, can share the report. We support SAML/SSO, RBAC, API keys, and integration with customer KMS. We'll email the security pack.
[04:45] Rene: Good. Encryption at rest/in transit and key separation is required. Also need ability to turn off data retention for certain customers.
[04:53] Marco: We can toggle retention per route and store only token-level metrics if requested. Key separation is supported via customer-managed KMS.
[05:05] Priya: On models — our preference is open models to avoid vendor lock-in. We saw quality improvements with some closed models but cost and governance are concerns. Which open models do you recommend for: 1) chat + tool calling, 2) multilingual, 3) long-context summarization?
[05:30] Marco: For chat + tool-calling, we recommend models that show good instruction-following and few hallucinations; depending on the time of eval, the top open ones are: Gemma-Alpha (hypothetical), Lumin-2, and Falcon-X variants. For multilingual tasks, models pre-trained on diverse corpora like Polyglot-7B and Lumin-2 show better behavior. For long-context, look at ResearchLongNet derivatives or models with efficient attention like Longformer forks. We also often use an ensemble approach — smaller fast model for routing + larger model for final answer generation.
[06:05] Tomás: How hard is it to switch models in production? We need pinning and canary rollouts.
[06:12] Marco: Redwood supports model pinning, versioning, and canary/A-B rollouts with automatic fallback to compatible model variants if capacity issues arise. The Console gives per-route dashboards and you can set routing policies by latency/cost.
[06:30] Priya: Tool-calling is critical — we need the model to call our internal SQL-generation tool and a document search API. Any examples of how Redwood handles tool calling?
[06:42] Marco: We provide function/tool calling primitives in the API. You define tool schemas and Redwood manages the structured calls. We also have a tool sandbox for testing triggers and retries. For latency-sensitive tool calls, we suggest localizing tool endpoints in the same VPC to avoid cross-region hops.
[07:03] Priya: Does tool-calling work across multilingual prompts?
[07:08] Marco: Generally yes. The model needs to produce the tool payload in a standard format; Redwood's function call wrapper handles parsing and can map multilingual prompts into the expected tool args. There are occasional edge cases with non-latin scripts — we recommend tests with your top languages.
[07:25] Rene: About logging tool payloads — can we redact sensitive fields automatically?
[07:30] Marco: Yes, we offer field-level redaction policies and can suppress storing full tool payloads. Those can be set per-route.
[07:40] Jess: Any questions on quantization and cost?
[07:45] Tomás: Yes — we want to push cost down without regressing quality. How aggressive can quantization be for our use cases?
[07:53] Marco: There's a quality curve. 4-bit quantization can work for many inference patterns, especially for reranking and embeddings. For instruction-following chat and tool-calling where hallucination risk is higher, we recommend mixed precision or calibrated quantization profiles which Redwood Optimize can suggest. We'll share example trade-off curves.
[08:20] Priya: For multilingual, we've seen tokenization issues — some models handle Spanish/Portuguese better than others. Can Redwood provide comparative metrics?
[08:32] Marco: Yes — in the eval we can run your sample prompts across candidate models and measure metric suite: BLEU-ish scores, hallucination rate, latency, tokenization anomalies. We'll include multilingual benchmarks.
[08:48] Priya: Great. On the pilot: we'd like to benchmark hosted vs dedicated for three flows: short chat, long summarization (50k), and tool-calling QPS of ~20.
[08:58] Jess: That sounds reasonable. Our pilot template is 2 weeks: week 1 baseline tests on hosted, week 2 dedicated reserved pool with same prompt set. We can capture latency p95, token cost, and quality metrics.
[09:12] Tomás: Will we need to open network to Redwood if Dedicated is in your cloud? We prefer VPC peering or private connectivity.
[09:20] Marco: Dedicated can be provisioned in a VPC with private peering, or Private mode lets you run the control plane separate and the inference in your VPC. We'll put the network diagram in the sec pack.
[09:32] Rene: Certification-wise, if we go Private, what's the support model and patch cadence?
[09:36] Marco: For Private deployments we provide an enterprise package: automated patch releases, but you control scheduling. For air-gapped on-prem, we ship update artifacts and an ops runbook. Support tiers include 24/7 for high-commit customers.
[09:50] Priya: Any notes about latency for long-context summarization when using retrieval+condense vs just large-context models?
[09:58] Marco: Retrieval+condense often reduces cost and latency, but adds complexity and potential context-mismatch errors. Large-context models avoid some of that but are more expensive per request. We can simulate both in the pilot.
[10:15] Jess: On commercial terms — if you commit to Dedicated for 12 months, we give a discount on reserved capacity and priority rollouts.
[10:24] Tomás: Rough numbers would help.
[10:26] Jess: I'll send a pricing sheet with example scenarios (hosted per-token, dedicated monthly commit tiers, private licensing).
[10:34] Priya: One more thing — we need to ensure model provenance and reproducibility for regulated outputs. Is there request-level model version and seed logging?
[10:45] Marco: Yes, per-request metadata includes model id, version, and RNG seed when applicable; all of that can be part of the audit trail.
[10:54] Rene: And retention of those logs is configurable?
[10:58] Marco: Correct, retention is configurable per-route and we can export to GCS or your SIEM.
[11:07] Priya: Regarding safety and hallucinations, do you offer guardrail layers or post-processing?
[11:13] Marco: Redwood has an optional response-safety pipeline: filters, model-based verification, and structured output enforcement. For tool-calling we also validate tool payloads against schema before execution.
[11:30] Tomás: How does function calling behave when the model produces ambiguous args?
[11:35] Marco: We have a confidence threshold and a review path — either ask-to-clarify or a fallback to human-in-the-loop. You can set that per-route.
[11:48] Priya: For the multilingual agent, latency is a bigger UX driver. If we use a smaller multilingual model for runtime and a larger model for post-hoc correctness checks, does Redwood support multi-model pipelines in a single route?
[12:05] Marco: Yes, you can chain calls or use Redwood's routing policy to pass outputs between models. The Console can visualize multi-model traces.
[12:18] Rene: Data residency: if we store embeddings in your managed service, where are they located?
[12:24] Marco: By default hosted is regional; we can pin regions and for Private you choose where storage resides. We can also support customer-managed embedding stores in your VPC for sensitive assets.
[12:38] Priya: Any gotchas with tokenization for Portuguese (pt-BR) — we've had worse outputs from some LLMs.
[12:44] Marco: We will run a tokenization and sensitivity test for pt-BR in the eval. Some tokenizers split clitics unexpectedly; we'll include that in the benchmark.
[12:58] Jess: Looping back to next steps — we'll share documentation pack and pricing, Marco will handle bench questionnaire. Priya, you'll send the prompt sets.
[13:10] Priya: Yes, we'll send 30 representative prompts across three flows, including Spanish and Portuguese.
[13:18] Tomás: We'll also provide expected qps and network diagrams.
[13:23] Rene: I'll review the security pack and get back with any follow-ups.
[13:29] Marco: For the pilot, do you have any preferred metrics for hallucination or QA scoring?
[13:35] Priya: We'll use a combined metric: correctness (binary), partial correctness (0.5), hallucination incidents per 100 responses, and a human rating for fluency.
[13:47] Marco: Good — we'll map those to an eval dashboard.
[14:00] Jess: Anything else before we wrap?
[14:05] Priya: Timeline: we want to kick pilot week of Dec 8. Is that feasible?
[14:10] Marco: Yes — we'll prioritize resource scheduling. Jess will send contracts and pricing.
[14:18] Jess: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the deck, security pack, and pilot plan.
[14:25] Priya: Appreciate it.

[47:30] End of recording.
